subtopic_detail: Umbilical granuloma after cord separation distinguished from omphalitis and umbilical remnants
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 3 week old boy, born at term and fully breastfed. His mother says the cord came away on day 9 and since then there has been a small moist pink lump at his belly button that keeps staining his singlet with clear yellowish fluid.

He feeds every three hours, has eight wet nappies a day and regained his birth weight by day 10. He has had no fever and no vomiting. His mother has been cleaning the area with cooled boiled water.

data_table.Examination: 5 mm soft pink pedunculated lesion arising from the umbilical base, no surrounding erythema or induration, no urine and no faeculent material expressed on gentle pressure, abdomen soft with no palpable mass
data_table.Growth: Weight on the 50th centile, tracking since birth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence oral cefalexin and review the umbilicus in 48 hours
options.rationale: Systemic antibiotics treat omphalitis, which requires periumbilical erythema, induration or systemic upset before it can be diagnosed, and none of those are present here. Treating a granuloma with antibiotics delays the definitive treatment while exposing a well infant to unnecessary drug risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical granuloma)

options.text: Arrange an abdominal ultrasound to assess the urachal remnant
options.rationale: A patent urachus leaks urine from the umbilicus and a vitellointestinal duct remnant leaks bowel content, neither of which was expressed on examination, so imaging for a remnant is not indicated. Imaging is reserved for persistent discharge after cautery or for a lesion that does not respond to two or three treatments. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical granuloma)

options.text: Apply silver nitrate cautery to the lesion and review in one week
options.rationale: A soft pink pedunculated lesion at the umbilical base with a serous discharge and no erythema is granulation tissue, and chemical cautery is the standard office treatment with the surrounding skin protected by a barrier. Most granulomas resolve after one or two applications, which is why review at one week is built into the plan. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical granuloma)

options.text: Refer to paediatric surgery for excision under general anaesthetic
options.rationale: Surgical excision is reserved for lesions that fail chemical treatment or that prove to be a true umbilical polyp, which is a firm bright red mucosal remnant rather than the soft pale granulation tissue described. Referring first exposes a well 3 week old to anaesthesia for a condition that usually resolves in the consulting room. (Source: RACGP: Umbilical lesions in infancy)

options.text: Take a swab for culture and start topical mupirocin three times daily
options.rationale: Swabs of the neonatal umbilicus grow skin and bowel flora in well infants and do not distinguish colonisation from infection, so a positive result here would mislead rather than guide. Topical antibacterials neither shrink granulation tissue nor treat the discharge it produces. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: An umbilical granuloma is overgrown granulation tissue at the base of the cord stump, appearing in the first weeks after separation and presenting as persistent moist serous discharge. The differential is short and each alternative has a discriminating feature: omphalitis brings periumbilical erythema and systemic upset, a patent urachus leaks urine, a vitellointestinal duct remnant leaks bowel content, and an umbilical polyp is firm bright red mucosa that does not respond to cautery. Clarifying which of these is present is entirely a bedside task and needs no imaging in a thriving infant. Missed omphalitis in a neonate progresses rapidly to necrotising fasciitis and portal vein thrombosis, which is why erythema changes the plan completely.
key_points: Soft pink pedunculated lesion with serous discharge and no erythema is granulation tissue, not infection
Silver nitrate cautery with barrier protection of surrounding skin is the office treatment of choice
Urine or faeculent discharge points to a urachal or vitellointestinal remnant and mandates imaging and surgical referral
Periumbilical erythema or systemic upset means omphalitis and requires intravenous antibiotics, not cautery
A lesion that fails two or three cautery treatments should be reassessed as a possible umbilical polyp
explanation.pearls: Silver nitrate burns normal skin, so smear petroleum jelly around the umbilicus before applying it and wipe the area with saline afterwards; a granuloma that has not shrunk after three weekly applications is probably an umbilical polyp and needs surgical referral.

subtopic_detail: Prolonged evening crying in a thriving six week old with a normal examination
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 6 week old boy whose parents say he cries inconsolably for about three hours most evenings, drawing his knees up and going red in the face, starting around 5 pm and settling by nine. It began at 3 weeks and is worse on some days than others.

His mother is exclusively breastfeeding and has already cut dairy from her own diet for a fortnight with no change. He feeds eagerly, has eight wet nappies a day, and passes soft yellow stool with no blood or mucus. His father says they are exhausted and have been told to try three different formulas.

data_table.Examination: Alert and settled during the consultation, abdomen soft and non-tender with no mass or organomegaly, no inguinal or scrotal swelling, no anal fissure, normal tone and reflexes, no corneal abrasion and no hair tourniquet on digits
data_table.Growth: Birth weight on the 50th centile, current weight on the 50th centile, length and head circumference tracking

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Explain the pattern, teach settling techniques and arrange early review
options.rationale: Crying that peaks in the late afternoon and evening, begins around 2 to 3 weeks and occurs in an infant who is thriving with a normal examination is the normal crying curve, which peaks at 6 to 8 weeks and resolves by 3 to 4 months. Structured explanation with settling strategies and planned review addresses the parental exhaustion that is the actual risk here, since inconsolable crying is the commonest trigger for abusive head trauma. (Source: RCH CPG: Crying baby)

options.text: Change to an extensively hydrolysed formula and review in two weeks
options.rationale: A hydrolysed formula trial is reserved for infants with other features of cow milk protein allergy such as blood or mucus in the stool, eczema, vomiting or faltering growth, none of which are present. Replacing breastfeeding with formula on this history removes its protective benefits without evidence of a food protein cause, particularly as maternal dairy exclusion has already failed. (Source: RCH CPG: Crying baby)

options.text: Commence an oral proton pump inhibitor and review him in four weeks
options.rationale: Randomised trials show acid suppression does not reduce crying in unsettled infants, and it is associated with increased rates of gastroenteritis, lower respiratory infection and fracture in infancy. Reflux is only implicated when there is genuine distress with feeds, back arching during feeding or faltering growth. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastro-oesophageal reflux in infants)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Gastro-oesophageal reflux in infants

options.text: Prescribe simethicone drops to be given before each evening feed
options.rationale: Simethicone has been tested against placebo in this setting and does not reduce crying duration, so it offers reassurance rather than effect. Recommending it also reinforces a gastrointestinal explanation the examination does not support. (Source: RCH CPG: Crying baby)

options.text: Arrange an abdominal ultrasound to exclude a structural abnormality
options.rationale: Imaging is indicated when the history or examination suggests an organic cause, such as bilious vomiting, a palpable mass, abdominal distension or episodic pallor with drawing up of the legs between periods of lethargy. A thriving infant with a normal abdomen and a predictable daily pattern does not warrant it. (Source: RCH CPG: Crying baby)

explanation.summary: Unsettled crying in early infancy follows a well described curve that begins at around 2 weeks, peaks at 6 to 8 weeks, is concentrated in the late afternoon and evening, and resolves by 3 to 4 months, and it affects roughly one in five infants at a level that prompts a consultation. The clinical task is to separate this from organic causes through a thorough history and a genuinely complete examination, which includes the eyes for a corneal abrasion, the digits for a hair tourniquet, the groin for an incarcerated hernia, the anus for a fissure and the growth chart. Once organic causes are excluded, the evidence does not support formula change, acid suppression, simethicone or anticholinergics, and management centres on explanation, practical settling strategies and support for parental fatigue. That support is not a soft option: inconsolable infant crying is the leading trigger for abusive head trauma, so asking directly how parents are coping and arranging early review is a safety intervention.
key_points: Crying peaks at 6 to 8 weeks and resolves by 3 to 4 months in most infants
Examination must include eyes, digits, groin, anus and the growth chart
Proton pump inhibitors and simethicone do not reduce crying and carry harms
Formula change is reserved for infants with other features of cow milk protein allergy
Inconsolable crying is the commonest trigger for abusive head trauma, so ask how parents are coping
explanation.pearls: Teach parents to put the baby down safely in the cot and walk away for a few minutes when they feel overwhelmed; naming this plan explicitly in the consultation is the single most effective thing said in a crying baby review.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Gastro-oesophageal reflux in infants

subtopic_detail: Easily reducible umbilical defect in a well toddler with a low risk of incarceration
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing an 18 month old girl whose parents point out a bulge at her belly button that has been present since the early weeks of life. It pushes out when she cries or strains and flattens when she lies quietly.

They have read that it can twist and are asking whether she needs an operation before she starts childcare. She has never vomited, has a good appetite and opens her bowels daily. They have been taping a coin over it at night on a relative's advice.

data_table.Examination: Soft symmetrical umbilical protrusion with a 12 mm fascial defect, completely and easily reducible with one finger, skin over it normal with no erythema or tenderness, abdomen otherwise soft with no distension
data_table.Growth: Weight and height both on the 75th centile and tracking

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for elective surgical repair before she commences childcare
options.rationale: Elective repair is offered for defects that persist beyond about 4 to 5 years of age, for very large or proboscoid defects, or after an episode of incarceration. Operating on an 18 month old commits her to a general anaesthetic for a defect that will most likely close on its own. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical hernia)

options.text: Apply a compression dressing over the defect until it has closed
options.rationale: Strapping, coins and binders have never been shown to accelerate closure and they cause skin maceration and pressure injury under an occlusive dressing. Advising the family to stop the taping they have already started is part of the consultation. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical hernia)

options.text: Request an abdominal ultrasound to measure the fascial defect size
options.rationale: The defect is measured clinically with a fingertip and imaging adds nothing to a diagnosis made by inspection and palpation. Ultrasound is reserved for an atypical periumbilical mass or when the swelling cannot be reduced. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical hernia)

options.text: Reassure, advise stopping the taping and review at 4 years of age
options.rationale: Umbilical hernias in children have a wide fascial ring and a low incarceration risk, unlike inguinal hernias, and the great majority close spontaneously by 4 to 5 years of age, with larger defects simply taking longer. The consultation therefore consists of reassurance, stopping ineffective home remedies, giving red flag advice about a tender irreducible lump with vomiting, and setting a review point at which referral becomes appropriate. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical hernia)

options.text: Refer urgently to the surgical team for assessment within 48 hours
options.rationale: Urgent referral is for a hernia that has become irreducible, tender or discoloured, or is accompanied by vomiting and abdominal distension, which signals incarceration or strangulation. This hernia reduces completely with one finger in a thriving, well child. (Source: RCH CPG: Umbilical hernia)

explanation.summary: Umbilical hernia results from incomplete closure of the fascial ring after cord separation and is present in a substantial proportion of infants, with a higher prevalence in those born preterm and in children of African ancestry. It behaves quite differently from an inguinal hernia: the neck is wide, incarceration is rare, and spontaneous closure occurs in the great majority by 4 to 5 years, so the standard approach is observation rather than repair. Families frequently arrive having tried coins, straps or binders, none of which work and all of which can damage the skin, so correcting that advice is part of the visit. The features that change the plan are a tender or irreducible lump, overlying skin change, vomiting or distension, all of which mandate urgent surgical assessment. Persistence beyond 4 to 5 years, a very large or proboscoid defect, or a previous incarceration are the usual indications for elective repair.
key_points: Wide necked defect with low incarceration risk, unlike inguinal hernia
Most close spontaneously by 4 to 5 years of age
Taping, coins and binders are ineffective and cause skin injury
Tenderness, irreducibility, vomiting or distension mandate urgent surgical review
Elective repair is for persistence beyond 4 to 5 years or a very large defect
explanation.pearls: An inguinal hernia in an infant is the opposite situation and should be referred for repair on the day it is diagnosed, because incarceration risk is highest in the first months of life and rises the longer repair is delayed.

sources.label: RACGP: Common surgical problems in childhood

subtopic_detail: Vulval soreness with scant discharge in a prepubertal girl with no bleeding or foreign body features
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 5 year old girl whose mother reports 6 weeks of on and off soreness and itch around the vulva, worse after swimming lessons and when she has been in her leotard all afternoon. There is a small amount of thin discharge on her underwear but no blood.

She wipes herself after using the toilet and often forgets to wash her hands. She has no urinary frequency or dysuria, no bedwetting, no weight loss and no behavioural change. Her mother has been using a bubble bath and a scented soap at bath time.

data_table.Examination: Diffuse erythema of the vulval skin and posterior fourchette with no excoriation, no bruising, no laceration and no bleeding, hymen intact and unremarkable on separation, no visible foreign material, no inguinal lymphadenopathy, no rash elsewhere
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for nitrites, leucocytes and blood

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe a 7 day course of oral cefalexin and review after treatment
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics are used when a specific bacterial cause is identified, most often group A streptococcus producing a bright red painful vulvitis often after a sore throat, or when a urinary tract infection is confirmed. Non-specific vulvovaginitis is not primarily an infective condition and antibiotics alter the flora without relieving it. (Source: RCH CPG: Vulvovaginitis)

options.text: Advise hygiene measures with a barrier ointment and review in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Prepubertal vulvovaginitis is an irritant condition arising from unoestrogenised thin vulval skin, proximity to the anus and exposure to soaps, bubble baths and damp clothing, so treatment is stopping the irritants, salt baths, loose cotton clothing, front to back wiping and a bland barrier ointment. Most children improve within weeks and the condition resolves entirely once oestrogenisation begins at puberty. (Source: RCH CPG: Vulvovaginitis)

options.text: Apply topical clotrimazole cream twice daily for two weeks and review
options.rationale: Candida is rare in prepubertal girls outside nappies because the unoestrogenised vagina lacks the glycogen that supports it, and it should prompt consideration of diabetes or recent antibiotics if genuinely present. Treating empirically for thrush in this age group usually treats the wrong organism. (Source: RCH CPG: Vulvovaginitis)

options.text: Refer to a paediatric gynaecologist for examination under anaesthetic
options.rationale: Examination under anaesthetic with vaginoscopy is indicated for persistent blood stained or offensive discharge suggesting a retained foreign body, for a suspected tumour, or for an injury that cannot otherwise be assessed. The examination here is normal apart from erythema, with no bleeding and no visible foreign material. (Source: RCH CPG: Vulvovaginitis)

options.text: Refer to the child protection unit for a formal forensic assessment
options.rationale: Vulval symptoms alone are not an indicator of abuse, and non-specific vulvovaginitis is common, but bruising, lacerations, bleeding, a sexually transmitted infection, disclosure or behavioural change would change that assessment entirely. Referring without any such feature medicalises a common problem while diverting a scarce service. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

explanation.summary: Non-specific vulvovaginitis is the commonest gynaecological problem of childhood and reflects anatomy and physiology rather than infection: the prepubertal vulva is thin, unoestrogenised, unprotected by labial fat or pubic hair, and sits close to the anus. Soaps, bubble baths, chlorinated water, damp swimwear or leotards and imperfect wiping technique all contribute, and the history in this case names several of them. Management is entirely conservative, and the great majority improve with irritant avoidance, salt baths and a barrier ointment, with complete resolution once puberty oestrogenises the epithelium. A swab is not routine but is taken when the vulva is bright red and painful, suggesting group A streptococcus, or when discharge is purulent. The findings that take the child out of this pathway are blood stained or offensive discharge, which suggests a retained foreign body, and any sign of trauma, a sexually transmitted infection or disclosure, which requires child protection assessment.
key_points: The condition is irritant rather than infective and reflects prepubertal vulval anatomy
Soaps, bubble baths, chlorinated water and damp clothing are the usual contributors
Candida is rare before puberty and suggests diabetes or recent antibiotics if present
Blood stained or offensive discharge suggests a retained foreign body needing vaginoscopy
Trauma, a sexually transmitted infection or disclosure require child protection assessment
explanation.pearls: A bright red, sharply demarcated, painful vulvitis, especially following a sore throat, is group A streptococcal vulvitis and needs a swab and oral penicillin rather than the conservative measures that treat the non-specific form.

subtopic_detail: Laryngomalacia complicated by faltering growth requiring airway endoscopy rather than observation
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4 month old boy referred with noisy breathing that began at 4 weeks of age. His mother describes a high pitched noise as he breathes in, worse when he lies on his back and when he feeds, and much quieter when he is on his tummy.

Feeds now take 45 minutes, during which he repeatedly pulls off the breast and goes red in the face. His weight has fallen from the 50th centile at birth to the 3rd centile.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 136 beats per minute, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 44 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 percent in room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Inspiratory stridor audible at rest, mild suprasternal recession, no barking cough, chest clear on auscultation, no cutaneous haemangioma on the head or neck, no dysmorphic features

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the parents and review when he is 12 months of age
options.rationale: Expectant management is right for mild laryngomalacia, defined by stridor without feeding difficulty, recession or growth failure, and this infant has all three. Waiting to 12 months accepts continued faltering growth at the age of fastest brain growth. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor)

options.text: Commence a proton pump inhibitor and thicken feeds for 6 weeks
options.rationale: Reflux frequently coexists with laryngomalacia and acid suppression is often used as an adjunct, but it does not relieve the supraglottic collapse that is causing the obstruction and it has not been shown to reverse growth failure in this setting. Committing to a 6 week trial defers the assessment that decides whether surgery is needed. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor)

options.text: Give oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg and observe for 3 hours
options.rationale: Corticosteroid treats the subglottic oedema of croup, which presents acutely with a barking cough and hoarse voice in a child usually over 6 months, not with 3 months of positional stridor. The near pair here is that croup and laryngomalacia both cause inspiratory stridor, but croup is acute and febrile while laryngomalacia is chronic and positional. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Arrange a chest radiograph to look for a vascular ring
options.rationale: A vascular ring produces biphasic stridor that is not positional and is often accompanied by feeding difficulty with solids, and a plain chest radiograph cannot exclude it in any case. The definitive test would be contrast imaging, and it is not the first step when the history points to a supraglottic cause. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor)

options.text: Refer for flexible laryngoscopy and paediatric airway assessment
options.rationale: Stridor with feeding difficulty and faltering growth defines moderate to severe disease, and awake flexible laryngoscopy confirms the supraglottic collapse and identifies the 15 to 20 per cent of infants with a second synchronous airway lesion. It is also the assessment that determines candidacy for supraglottoplasty, which reliably reverses the growth failure. (Source: RCH CPG: Stridor)

explanation.summary: Laryngomalacia accounts for the majority of chronic stridor in infants, typically starting in the first weeks of life, worsening over the first few months and resolving by 12 to 24 months. The history is characteristic: inspiratory stridor that is worse supine, worse with feeding or crying and better prone. Severity is graded by what the obstruction is costing the infant, so feeding difficulty, recession, cyanosis, apnoea or faltering growth move a child from watchful waiting to endoscopic assessment. A synchronous second airway lesion is present in a significant minority, which is another reason the airway is looked at rather than assumed.
key_points: Positional inspiratory stridor from the first weeks of life is laryngomalacia until proven otherwise
Mild disease is stridor alone and needs only review and parental reassurance
Feeding difficulty, recession, apnoea or faltering growth define moderate to severe disease
Flexible laryngoscopy identifies synchronous airway lesions in 15 to 20 per cent
Supraglottoplasty is effective for severe disease and reverses growth failure
explanation.pearls: Stridor that is present from birth rather than appearing at 2 to 6 weeks, or that is biphasic rather than inspiratory, argues against laryngomalacia and points towards vocal cord palsy or subglottic stenosis, which need endoscopy regardless of severity.

subtopic_detail: Nocturnal perianal itch in a school aged child requiring treatment of the whole household
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 6 year old boy whose mother reports 3 weeks of intense itching around his bottom, always after he goes to bed, waking him most nights and leaving him irritable at school. She looked with a torch two nights ago and saw what she describes as small moving white threads.

His 4 year old sister has started scratching too. He has had no diarrhoea, no weight loss, no fever and no blood in the stool. The family has not travelled.

data_table.Examination: Perianal excoriation from scratching with no fissure, no fistula and no perianal erythema suggesting streptococcal infection, abdomen soft and non-tender, no rash elsewhere
data_table.Growth: Weight and height tracking along the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Treat the whole household and repeat the dose after two weeks
options.rationale: A nocturnal perianal itch with visible motile white threads is enterobiasis, and because eggs are shed onto bedding and household surfaces and reinfection is the rule, everyone in the house is treated simultaneously whether or not they have symptoms. The dose is repeated after 2 weeks because the treatment kills adult worms but not eggs, and that interval covers the maturation of any eggs ingested around the first dose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Treat the index child only with a single dose and review at 4 weeks
options.rationale: Treating one member of a household leaves an untreated reservoir, and reinfection from siblings and shared bedding follows within weeks, which is exactly what is beginning with his sister. It also omits the repeat dose that covers eggs surviving the first treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Send three stool specimens for microscopy before starting any treatment
options.rationale: Stool microscopy is insensitive for this infection because the female worm deposits eggs on perianal skin rather than in faeces, so a negative result is common and misleading. When confirmation is genuinely needed the adhesive tape test applied to the perianal skin on waking is the appropriate investigation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Apply a topical corticosteroid nightly for one week and review after
options.rationale: A topical corticosteroid may settle the excoriation but does nothing to eradicate the organism causing the itch, which will continue and spread through the household. It also risks masking a perianal streptococcal infection, which is the main mimic and requires antibiotics instead. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Advise hygiene measures alone and treat only if symptoms persist
options.rationale: Hygiene measures such as morning showering, nail trimming and hot washing of bedding reduce reinfection and are part of the advice, but they are an adjunct rather than a substitute for treatment. Withholding treatment leaves an itchy child losing sleep and an expanding household reservoir. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Enterobius vermicularis is the most common helminth infection in Australian children and spreads by the faecal oral route when eggs deposited on perianal skin at night are transferred by scratching to hands, bedding, toys and surfaces, where they remain viable for up to 3 weeks. The presentation is characteristic enough to treat on history alone: intense perianal itch confined to the night, often with visible motile white threads, and frequently with affected siblings. Because reinfection within a household is the norm, everyone living in the house is treated at the same time, and the dose is repeated after 2 weeks since the treatment is active against adult worms but not eggs. Hygiene measures reduce recurrence and matter, particularly morning showering to remove eggs laid overnight, trimming nails, and washing bedding and nightclothes in hot water at the time of treatment. Vulvovaginitis and secondary bacterial infection from scratching are the usual complications, and migration causing appendicitis or genitourinary infection is rare.
key_points: Nocturnal perianal itch with visible white threads is enough to treat without testing
Treat all household members simultaneously, symptomatic or not
Repeat the dose after 2 weeks because treatment does not kill eggs
Stool microscopy is insensitive; the adhesive tape test is used if confirmation is needed
Hot washing of bedding and morning showering reduce reinfection
explanation.pearls: Threadworm is a recognised cause of vulvovaginitis in prepubertal girls, so consider it in any girl with vulval itch that is markedly worse at night, and treat the household rather than persisting with topical measures.

subtopic_detail: Positional plagiocephaly distinguished from lambdoid craniosynostosis by head shape and ear position
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 5 month old boy whose parents noticed flattening at the back of his head from about 3 months of age. He sleeps supine, dislikes tummy time, and was treated with physiotherapy for a right sided head tilt at 8 weeks.

His parents want to know whether he needs an operation. He is smiling, rolling front to back and reaching for objects with both hands.

data_table.Examination viewed from above: Right occipital flattening with the right ear displaced anteriorly and mild right frontal prominence, giving a parallelogram outline
data_table.Skull examination: Anterior fontanelle open and soft, no palpable ridge over any suture, no bulging behind the ear
data_table.Growth: Head circumference on the 50th centile and tracking

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the skull with 3 dimensional views
options.rationale: Three dimensional computed tomography is the confirmatory test for craniosynostosis once the head shape and ear position suggest it, and it delivers a meaningful radiation dose to an infant brain. The parallelogram shape with an anteriorly displaced ear and no sutural ridge argues against synostosis, so the test would be ordered to confirm a diagnosis the examination has already made unlikely. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

options.text: Refer urgently to the craniofacial unit for surgical assessment
options.rationale: Urgent craniofacial referral is for a trapezoid head shape, a palpable sutural ridge, a mastoid bulge or a head circumference crossing centiles, which together signal fused sutures and rising intracranial pressure. None of those are present, and urgent referral here displaces a child who genuinely needs the appointment. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

options.text: Advise repositioning and tummy time with physiotherapy review
options.rationale: A parallelogram head with the ipsilateral ear pushed forward, a mobile open fontanelle and no ridge is deformational plagiocephaly, which responds to repositioning, supervised awake prone time and treatment of the residual torticollis that is driving the preferential head position. Most cases improve substantially by 12 months once the infant sits and spends less time supine. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

options.text: Refer for a moulding helmet orthosis to be fitted this month
options.rationale: Helmet therapy is a second line option considered for severe deformity that has not responded to several months of active repositioning, and randomised evidence shows no meaningful advantage over natural improvement for mild to moderate cases while causing skin irritation and considerable cost. Offering it before a repositioning trial skips the treatment that works for most infants. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

options.text: Request skull radiographs to assess the lambdoid suture
options.rationale: Plain skull radiographs are insensitive for partial sutural fusion and a normal film would not exclude synostosis, so a test with this performance cannot safely reassure. The distinction between deformational plagiocephaly and lambdoid synostosis is made by head shape and ear position at the bedside. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

explanation.summary: Deformational plagiocephaly became common after supine sleeping was adopted for sudden infant death prevention and is benign, whereas lambdoid craniosynostosis is rare and needs surgery. The two are separated by geometry rather than imaging: deformational flattening pushes the ipsilateral ear and forehead forward, producing a parallelogram viewed from above, while lambdoid fusion pulls the ear posteriorly and inferiorly with contralateral frontal bossing and a mastoid bulge, producing a trapezoid. A palpable ridge over the suture, a closing fontanelle or a head circumference crossing centiles shifts the assessment towards synostosis. Torticollis is the usual driver of the preferential head position and must be treated or the flattening recurs despite repositioning advice.
key_points: Parallelogram with the ear pushed anteriorly is deformational, trapezoid with the ear posterior and inferior is lambdoid synostosis
A palpable sutural ridge or mastoid bulge is the physical sign of synostosis
Treating coexisting torticollis is essential or repositioning fails
Helmet therapy is second line and has not outperformed repositioning for mild to moderate deformity
Three dimensional computed tomography confirms synostosis but is not a screening test
explanation.pearls: Head circumference crossing centiles upwards in an infant with an abnormal head shape suggests multi suture fusion with raised intracranial pressure and warrants craniofacial referral within days rather than a repositioning trial.

sources.label: RACGP: Abnormal head shape in infants

subtopic_detail: Distal radial buckle fracture treated with a removable splint rather than cast immobilisation
stem:
You are the emergency department resident seeing a 7 year old boy who fell from the monkey bars onto an outstretched right hand two hours ago. He is holding the wrist and says it hurts when he tries to turn a doorknob.

He has been able to move all his fingers since the fall and there is no other injury. His parents are asking how long he will be in plaster.

data_table.Examination: Minimal swelling over the distal radius with no deformity, no tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox or over the distal ulna, full finger movement, capillary refill under 2 seconds, normal sensation in median, ulnar and radial distributions
data_table.Radiograph: Buckling of the dorsal cortex of the distal radial metaphysis with the volar cortex intact, no angulation, distal radioulnar joint congruent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Below elbow backslab and fracture clinic review within one week
options.rationale: A backslab plus clinic review is the pathway for a complete or angulated fracture that could displace and therefore needs a check radiograph. A buckle fracture has an intact opposite cortex and is inherently stable, so it cannot displace and the review visit finds nothing to act on. (Source: RCH CPG: Distal radius and ulna fractures)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Distal radius and ulna fractures

options.text: Full below elbow cast for 6 weeks with repeat radiographs at 3 weeks
options.rationale: Six weeks of casting is the treatment duration for a complete forearm fracture and overtreats an injury that heals in 3 to 4 weeks, while adding joint stiffness, muscle wasting, cast complications and lost school and sport time. Repeat imaging of a stable buckle fracture does not change management. (Source: RCH CPG: Distal radius and ulna fractures)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Distal radius and ulna fractures

options.text: Closed reduction under procedural sedation then apply a cast
options.rationale: Reduction is indicated for angulation beyond the age related acceptable limits, and this fracture has no angulation to correct. Sedating a child to reduce an undisplaced compression injury exposes them to airway and cardiovascular risk for no gain. (Source: RCH CPG: Distal radius and ulna fractures)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Distal radius and ulna fractures

options.text: Sling for comfort and repeat radiographs in 10 days to reassess
options.rationale: A sling gives no wrist support and leaves the child with unnecessary pain during the 3 to 4 weeks of healing, while repeat radiographs of a stable injury add radiation without altering the plan. The near pair to keep straight is the scaphoid fracture, which does justify a splint and repeat imaging because it is often radiographically occult, and snuffbox tenderness is absent here. (Source: RCH CPG: Distal radius and ulna fractures)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Distal radius and ulna fractures

options.text: Removable wrist splint for 3 to 4 weeks without routine follow up
options.rationale: Randomised trials show a removable splint gives equal or better function and pain scores than casting for buckle fractures, with faster return to activity and no risk of late displacement because the opposite cortex is intact. Parents are told to use it for comfort, wean it as pain settles, and return only if pain persists beyond 4 weeks. (Source: RCH CPG: Distal radius and ulna fractures)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Distal radius and ulna fractures

explanation.summary: A buckle or torus fracture is a compression injury of the metaphyseal cortex in which the opposite cortex remains intact, which makes it mechanically stable and unable to displace. Australian and international practice has moved decisively from cast immobilisation to a removable splint with no routine follow up, supported by randomised evidence showing equivalent pain and function with faster return to normal activity. The key task for the treating doctor is distinguishing a buckle fracture from a greenstick or complete fracture, where one cortex is actually broken and the injury can angulate. The other trap is the scaphoid injury, where snuffbox tenderness with normal initial films warrants splinting and repeat assessment because the fracture is often occult at presentation.
key_points: Buckle fracture means an intact opposite cortex and therefore inherent stability
Removable splint for 3 to 4 weeks matches casting on pain and function in randomised trials
Routine follow up radiographs are not required because displacement cannot occur
A broken cortex on either side makes it a greenstick or complete fracture needing casting
Snuffbox tenderness changes the pathway regardless of the radiograph appearance
explanation.pearls: Tell families that the splint is worn for comfort and weaned as pain settles rather than for a fixed period, and that pain persisting beyond 4 weeks is the only reason to return; this single instruction removes the routine review visit entirely.

subtopic_detail: Toe walking with calf hypertrophy and a positive Gowers sign requiring creatine kinase measurement
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 4 year old boy referred because he walks on his toes most of the time. His parents were told at his 3 year check that it was habit and that he would grow out of it.

He walked independently at 17 months, still falls several times a day, and climbs stairs one foot at a time holding the rail. He speaks in full sentences and is toilet trained. He was born at term with no perinatal problems.

data_table.Gait and lower limb examination: Walks on the toes of both feet with intermittent heel contact, bulky firm calves bilaterally, ankle dorsiflexion 5 degrees beyond neutral with the knee extended
data_table.Neurological examination: Rises from the floor by turning prone and pushing up on his own thighs, normal tone, reflexes present and symmetrical, no ankle clonus, plantar responses downgoing, no spinal dimple or hairy patch

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Refer to physiotherapy for a serial casting programme of both ankles
options.rationale: Serial casting treats fixed equinus contracture in idiopathic toe walking, and this boy still achieves dorsiflexion beyond neutral, so there is no contracture to stretch. More importantly, casting a child with an undiagnosed myopathy causes disuse weakness and can precipitate loss of ambulation. (Source: RCH CPG: Toe walking)

options.text: Measure the serum creatine kinase and review the result urgently
options.rationale: Calf hypertrophy, a positive Gowers sign, late independent walking and frequent falls in a boy of this age point to Duchenne muscular dystrophy, in which creatine kinase is typically elevated 10 to 100 times the upper limit of normal and is the screening test that triggers genetic confirmation. It is cheap, immediate, and the single test that changes the diagnosis from a gait habit to a progressive neuromuscular disease. (Source: RCH CPG: Toe walking)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and spinal cord
options.rationale: Central imaging looks for a tethered cord or an upper motor neuron cause, both of which produce increased tone, brisk reflexes, sustained clonus or upgoing plantars, and all of those are normal here. A positive Gowers sign with preserved reflexes localises to muscle rather than to cord or brain. (Source: RCH CPG: Toe walking)

options.text: Refer for orthopaedic tendo Achilles lengthening assessment now
options.rationale: Surgical lengthening is considered for persistent idiopathic toe walking with fixed contracture after conservative treatment has failed, in a child whose muscle disease has already been excluded. Operating on a boy with an undiagnosed dystrophy accelerates functional decline. (Source: RCH CPG: Toe walking)

options.text: Request nerve conduction studies of both lower limbs this week
options.rationale: Nerve conduction studies interrogate peripheral nerve and would be appropriate for a hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy, which characteristically produces pes cavus, distal wasting and absent ankle reflexes. This boy has proximal weakness with bulky calves and preserved reflexes, the opposite pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Toe walking)

explanation.summary: Idiopathic toe walking is a diagnosis of exclusion and requires normal motor milestones, normal strength and a normal neurological examination before the label is applied. The conditions that masquerade as it are cerebral palsy, which adds spasticity and brisk reflexes, tethered cord, which may add bladder symptoms or a cutaneous marker, and Duchenne muscular dystrophy, which adds calf pseudohypertrophy, a positive Gowers sign and delayed motor milestones in a boy. The average age at diagnosis of Duchenne remains around 4 to 5 years despite symptoms from age 2, and toe walking labelled as habit is one of the recurring reasons for that delay. Early diagnosis matters because corticosteroids started before significant decline prolong ambulation, and because it allows genetic counselling before another affected pregnancy.
key_points: Idiopathic toe walking requires normal milestones and a normal neurological examination
Calf pseudohypertrophy with a positive Gowers sign in a boy means creatine kinase today
Creatine kinase in Duchenne is typically 10 to 100 times the upper limit of normal
Spasticity, brisk reflexes or clonus point to cerebral palsy rather than muscle disease
Casting or tendon lengthening in undiagnosed dystrophy hastens loss of ambulation
explanation.pearls: A boy who is not yet walking at 18 months, or who has a creatine kinase above 1000 units per litre at any age, needs dystrophin gene testing; corticosteroids begun before the plateau of motor function extend independent walking by 2 to 3 years.

subtopic_detail: Craniocervical junction stenosis in achondroplasia presenting with central apnoea and long tract signs
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 9 month old boy with genetically confirmed achondroplasia in the growth clinic. Over the past 6 weeks his parents have noticed pauses in his breathing during sleep, each ending with a snort, and they feel he has become floppier when they pick him up.

He is not yet sitting unsupported. His head circumference is tracking along the 75th centile of the achondroplasia specific chart.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 128 beats per minute, blood pressure 88/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 percent in room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Neurological examination: Central hypotonia with head lag on pull to sit, brisk knee and ankle reflexes, four beats of sustained ankle clonus on the right, plantar responses upgoing bilaterally
data_table.Upper airway examination: Tonsils small, no adenoidal facies, no stridor at rest

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure that hypotonia and delayed motor milestones are expected
options.rationale: Mild hypotonia and motor delay are indeed typical in achondroplasia, which is exactly why the abnormal findings must be separated from the expected ones. Sustained clonus and upgoing plantars are never part of the natural history and signal cord compression. (Source: RCH CPG: Achondroplasia)

options.text: Arrange overnight oximetry at home and review in three months
options.rationale: Home oximetry detects desaturation but cannot distinguish central from obstructive events, which is the whole question when craniocervical compression is suspected. A three month delay in a child with long tract signs risks irreversible cord injury or sudden death. (Source: RCH CPG: Achondroplasia)

options.text: Refer for adenotonsillectomy to treat obstructive sleep apnoea
options.rationale: Obstructive sleep apnoea is common in achondroplasia from midface hypoplasia and adenotonsillar tissue, but the tonsils are small here and obstruction does not cause pyramidal signs. Operating without characterising the apnoea leaves an untreated cord compression and subjects the child to an anaesthetic with an unstable craniocervical junction. (Source: RCH CPG: Achondroplasia)

options.text: Arrange craniocervical junction imaging and a polysomnogram
options.rationale: Foramen magnum stenosis is the leading cause of death in infants with achondroplasia, and the combination of new central apnoea with hyperreflexia, sustained clonus and upgoing plantars is its presentation. Magnetic resonance imaging defines the compression while polysomnography separates central from obstructive events, and together they determine whether decompression is needed. (Source: RCH CPG: Achondroplasia)

options.text: Request cervical spine radiographs in flexion and extension
options.rationale: Dynamic radiographs assess atlantoaxial instability, which belongs to conditions such as Down syndrome and the mucopolysaccharidoses rather than to achondroplasia, where the problem is bony narrowing at the foramen magnum. Plain films cannot show the cord or the degree of compression. (Source: RCH CPG: Achondroplasia)

explanation.summary: Achondroplasia results from a gain of function variant in the fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 gene and causes rhizomelic short stature, macrocephaly, midface hypoplasia and a narrow foramen magnum. Infants normally show mild hypotonia and delayed gross motor milestones, so the clinical skill is separating that expected pattern from cord compression, which adds hyperreflexia, sustained clonus, upgoing plantars and central apnoea. Sudden unexplained death in the first two years of life has historically affected a small but significant proportion of infants with achondroplasia and is largely attributable to unrecognised craniocervical compression. Structured surveillance with neurological examination, sleep study and imaging in the first year is the response to that risk, and decompression is effective when compression is found.
key_points: Hypotonia and motor delay are expected, but hyperreflexia, clonus and upgoing plantars never are
Foramen magnum stenosis is the leading cause of infant death in achondroplasia
Central apnoea points to brainstem compression, obstructive apnoea to midface and adenotonsillar narrowing
Polysomnography is required because oximetry cannot separate central from obstructive events
Head circumference must be plotted on achondroplasia specific charts, not standard charts
explanation.pearls: In achondroplasia, plot growth on condition specific charts and treat any new central apnoea or long tract sign as foramen magnum compression until magnetic resonance imaging says otherwise; suboccipital decompression reverses the apnoea in most affected infants.
